# tryharness

Harness Relay: turn the coding agents installed on this machine into your personal swarm with [Harness](https://tryharness.ai):

```sh
npx tryharness
```

Supports the Node.js 18, 20, 22, and 24 release lines.

That one command signs this computer in to your Harness account (one page in the browser: your
email, then Connect), lists the agents installed here with the ones that are signed in already
ticked, connects the ones you keep, installs the Harness daemon as a user-level login
service (launchd on macOS, a systemd user service on Linux, a Task Scheduler logon task
on Windows; all without elevation), validates readiness, and starts indexing existing
coding sessions locally in SQLite. Setup returns as soon as the daemon is ready; indexing continues in the
background and does not require an open Harness tab.

JSONL histories are streamed from beginning to end and only normalized conversation
records are retained. Source-file size does not truncate recall; long read results are
paged when Harness displays them.

The command is idempotent; run it again to repair a configuration. Your swarm holds only the
agents you picked: `npx tryharness agents` shows who is in it and who can be added,
`npx tryharness agents add [agent]` adds one (with no name, pick from the ones found here) and
`npx tryharness agents remove <agent>` takes one out. The buddy's settings has the same, under
Your swarm and Add an agent. A new account gets $20 of Harness credit once its first computer
is running Harness.

## Coding agents and existing work

Local execution supports Claude Code, Codex, Pi and OpenCode through their native
interfaces; Cursor (`cursor-agent acp`), Grok Build (`grok agent stdio`) and
Antigravity (`agy_acp_server.par`, `.exe` on Windows) through ACP; and Muse Code
(`muse serve`) through MSP. Each needs its own installation and authentication.
T3 is optional. Grok Build and Muse Code are separate from hosted Grok Bot and Muse.
Muse Code's SDK requires Node 20 or newer and is pinned to 1.4.11; incompatible
handshakes fail without substituting another agent. New protocol adapters do not
provide Harness's restricted or read-only execution contract.

An executable outside PATH can be selected in `~/.harness/config.json`, preserving
the rest of that file:

```json
{
  "agentCommands": {
    "cursor": { "command": "/absolute/path/to/cursor-agent", "args": ["acp"] }
  },
  "acpAgents": [
    {
      "id": "acp-example",
      "name": "My installed ACP agent",
      "command": "/absolute/path/to/agent",
      "args": ["acp"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Custom IDs start with `acp-`. Restart the daemon after adding a custom agent.
Registry packages are not automatically downloaded or installed. Model and effort
overrides must be offered by the actual protocol; otherwise the run refuses the
override. Muse preserves its configured permission policy; its optional
`agentCommands["muse-code"].approvalMode` selects an existing native mode.
An explicit model refresh now reads ACP model selectors and Muse's `model/list`
through disposable connections. Discovery submits no inference prompt. Automatic
startup refresh leaves these protocol sessions alone. Missing selectors and
unknown effort capabilities stay unavailable; overrides are checked again against
the opened session. Native session-history parsers and terminal reopen commands
still cover the original four agents. Muse requires the negotiated `sessionMcp`
capability and injects Harness tools into its owned session. Continuations resume
the exact durable native session; a model change is applied and read back while
that session is idle. ACP and Muse native permission requests appear in the buddy
and paired surfaces with only the agent's offered one-time choices. Decisions
are pinned to the live run and current request; Stop cancels a pending decision.
Muse native questionnaires remain unadvertised; agents can ask through Harness's
existing task-question path.

After approving Harness's T3 connection, existing T3 work appears in the ordinary
thread list and buddy canvas, including explicit delegated and native children.
The connection catalog includes custom provider instances, models and unavailable
providers with their reasons. Messages and Stop act on original root sessions;
Stop is pinned to the observed run. Delegated children open in their original
environment and remain controlled through their parent. Read-only grants permit
inspection. A lost action receipt is held for inspection rather than replayed.

The buddy's Following view keeps selected outside sessions alongside Harness work;
All discovers the rest. Followed work with words the person has not read carries a
dot. Reading a thread to its end records that version as read on the computer,
shared by paired surfaces; agents starting or stopping work do not change it, new
words, a new question or a later child update do. The thread then opens at a "New
since you looked" rule. Send to… on an agent's message puts it, with its source and
time, in the chosen thread's composer, the menu naming that thread's participants;
it stays an editable draft until the person sends it. Web/PiP thread views work the
same way. Nothing infers hidden connections or exports whole conversations.

Add existing work keeps original sessions beside a Harness objective, under the
thread's Related, in the buddy and paired web/PiP views. These references are
private to the person. Linked
updates bring the objective back into Following; revocation drops cached titles
and results. Use result here prepares an attributed draft. In an open PiP thread,
Use selected page text previews the permitted selection, address and capture time;
Add to reply preserves existing reply text and edits. The person's Send shares it
with the shown thread participants. Page context Pause prevents a new read.

Which agents are available depends on what is installed on the computer. Native
session authentication still requires each agent’s own setup.

## Daemon ownership

`lib/daemon.mjs` assembles features in `startDaemon` and connects the local control
socket and authenticated bridge. Features own their state and command handling:

| Module | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| `sessionIndex.mjs` | History scans, the OpenCode helper and targeted refreshes |
| `sessionControl.mjs` | Live sessions, app locations, Open plans and session messages |
| `runAuthority.mjs` | Prompt identity, workspace coverage and standing permission |
| `actorRoster.mjs` | Available agents, setup health and cards |
| `taskRuns.mjs` | Run records, output paging, restart recovery and execution identity |
| `models.mjs` | Agent catalogs, saved/run choices, agent settings and complete model/effort selections |
| `harnessModel.mjs` | Harness's own pick: a provider (Harness credits or a kept key or endpoint), a model of Harness's catalog there, and what a thread task carries for it |
| `roomPage.mjs` | One page of a thread's room, newest first, as every agent reads it (`read_room`, Harness's `thread_posts`) |
| `bridge.mjs` | Authenticated socket, requests, feature negotiation, heartbeat, reconnects and outage history |
| `threadRuns.mjs` | Durable pending wakes, fresh briefs, T3 continuity and worktree settlement |
| `runWorker.mjs` | Authorized board execution, workspace slots, holds, requeues and receipts |
| `boardFiles.mjs` | File storage, disclosure, redaction and file commands; `boardFileCommands.mjs` is its private command adapter |
| `goalCommands.mjs`, `taskCommands.mjs` | Goal/room operations and task lifecycle operations |
| `boardThreads.mjs`, `boardWatches.mjs`, `boardTools.mjs` | Messages between friends, watch/digest commands and local tool commands |
| `boardAccess.mjs` | Plain hosted-call policy and metadata-only responses |
| `connectors.mjs`, `connectorAuth.mjs` | Local app credentials, OAuth, discovered tools, scoped agent grants and durable operation receipts |

`createModelRouter` returns the complete run selection, including model, effort,
provenance and any fallback explanation. It owns the precedence of a run's explicit
pick, the person's saved choice or Auto, and the agent's own settings. Missing
settings stay null. The worker records and executes the result without resolving
defaults again; `runner.mjs` and `t3.mjs` translate it for their execution formats.
Cards and model listings read agent settings through the same model module.

`boardCommands.mjs` establishes the common request context and dispatches to the
feature owner. Dispatch grants no authority: each feature still checks identity,
permissions, versions and sharing before acting. `daemon.mjs` wires thread execution
and transport through their owners; feature handlers do not own socket retry state.

Pending thread calls use the existing local metadata store. After restart, an already
queued wake keeps its later handoff in the fresh brief. An interrupted run remains
unknown. A later call for that interrupted agent becomes a held wake and the thread
asks for Start, so recovery preserves the request without replaying unknown effects.

`lib/boardProtocol.json` owns command names, routing, protocol/inbox versions,
metadata fields and the separate grants for each caller surface. Node consumers use
`boardProtocol.mjs`; the Harness web app reads the same JSON; the Rust desktop
adapter embeds the JSON at build time. A surface uses only its own list: adding a
command to the catalog does not enable it for any caller. Browser and hosted Harness
grants deliberately differ. When adding a command, update its owner and only the
intended surface grants, then exercise that caller's runtime path.

## Operations

When a newer release is published, home tells you once, naming every computer behind it. The buddy's Settings shows
each computer's version with an Update button under Your devices, and `tryharness status` gives the command. Nothing
is fetched until you ask: Update runs the signed `tryharness upgrade` on that computer.

```sh
npx tryharness status
npx tryharness doctor
npx tryharness sync --agent codex
npx tryharness task <run-id> --follow
npx tryharness logs --follow
npx tryharness board
npx tryharness board post --for claude-code --objective "Port the parser" --file ./brief.md
npx tryharness uninstall
```

`status` is the normal health view. `doctor` verifies pairing, the login service, the
daemon, the bridge, the database, and agent discovery. `sync` requests a background
rescan; it is diagnostic, not part of normal setup. `uninstall` removes the app, the service and
Harness's setup in every agent, and keeps the board, history and keys in `~/.harness`;
`uninstall --everything` deletes those too.

Delegated coding tasks start when the user presses Start on Harness's proposal card, or
at once when standing permission covers the folder (see Task board); either way the task is
posted on the machine's board under the run id. Native CLI runners use their
existing full-authority modes; ACP and Muse preserve native session policies and
surface interactive one-time permission decisions. Every run uses the exact
absolute working directory shown on that card; Harness never falls back to the
user's home directory. The card immediately shows a
`npx tryharness task <run-id> --follow` command for watching the machine-local raw output
in a terminal. For the original four native agents, the card and follow command
print their native session command once its id arrives, including while active.
Other protocols keep their native session identity without inventing a terminal
reopen command.

## Vault

Your keys, tokens and passwords are kept on this computer, in 1claw's open
local-vault format (`~/.harness/vault.enc`, sealed with `~/.harness/vault-key`).
Agents use them through `use_secret`: the relay puts the value into the request,
sends it only to the websites you named for it, and gives the agent the answer with
the value replaced by a marker. An agent uses a secret only once you allow it; one
that asks first shows up in `npx tryharness vault`, the buddy and the dashboard.

```sh
npx tryharness vault                                   # what is kept, who asks, who may use what
npx tryharness vault add fly-token --hosts api.fly.io  # typed hidden or piped; never on the command line
npx tryharness vault allow codex fly-token
npx tryharness vault runs codex fly-token FLY_API_TOKEN [--elsewhere]
npx tryharness vault backup you@example.com [--bring-in]
npx tryharness vault share fly-token --hours 24 --uses 1
```

`runs` puts the value in that agent's runs as an environment variable: the agent can
read it there, and what its runs say is cleaned of it. With `--elsewhere` it also
goes, sealed, to runs on your other computers; otherwise it stays in runs here. Your
other computers use the vault on your home computer. Backup keeps a copy in your
1claw account (the email you sign in to 1claw with; a new email makes an account,
and an account that signs in with a wallet cannot back up yet); a new computer gets
it back by turning backup on with the same email. A 1claw payment request stops the backup:
nothing is ever paid.

## App connections

Connect apps once on this computer, then grant particular operations to agents:

```sh
npx tryharness connections catalog
npx tryharness connections add linear
npx tryharness connections list
npx tryharness connections tools <connection-id>
npx tryharness connections grant <connection-id> --agent codex --tool <listed-tool> --effect read
npx tryharness connections operations
npx tryharness connections approve <operation-id>
npx tryharness connections revoke <connection-id>
```

The catalog includes Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, Notion and Linear. Google uses
its public APIs, without Workspace MCP Developer Preview enrollment. Configure a
Google **Desktop app** OAuth client in the daemon environment with
`HARNESS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and `HARNESS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`, or enter the client
fields in settings. The client must have the Calendar/Gmail APIs enabled and the
appropriate Google consent/verification configuration. Read access is the default;
settings offers explicit additional consent for calendar edits, Gmail drafts, or
Gmail sending.
Calendar edits/deletions require a last-read etag. Draft approvals display the
complete decoded MIME content. Calendar effects and saved drafts include an
independent read-back receipt; an unavailable check stays unverified. Gmail sends
the exact approved MIME message bytes with their recipients and content. Sending
requires its own provider scope and an agent's `send` grant. A sent-copy check
verifies those contents in Gmail; delivery to recipients remains unverified. An
uncertain send is never automatically repeated.

Notion and Linear advertise dynamic OAuth registration. Slack requires an internal
or Marketplace-published OAuth app, its client secret and an approved callback.
Advanced `--client-id`, `--client-secret-env`, `--scope` and `--callback` options
support registered clients. A fixed callback must be
`http://127.0.0.1:PORT/callback`; otherwise Relay allocates a loopback port for that
sign-in. Finish sign-in on the computer running Relay. These presets and public
metadata probes do not certify live authenticated provider behavior.

A custom server uses `connections add <name> --url <url>`; an existing access token
can be read from an environment variable with `--token-env <name>`. Credentials
rest encrypted on this computer and never go to agents. `connections reconnect
<id>` signs in again and clears the previous grants, since a new sign-in can select
a different account. Disconnect removes stored credentials and grants; refreshing
discovery cannot reconnect a disconnected account. Remove the app in the provider's
own settings as well to revoke the upstream OAuth authorization.
New grants do not restore an agent's access to operation content from an earlier
authority revision or a previously connected account.

Every agent uses the `connection` MCP tool to list its granted connections, inspect
their tools, request an operation and retrieve its result. Harness chat/PiP uses
the same tool under the `harness` identity. A hosted client separately needs the
`connections` token scope (manual token or explicit OAuth consent) and a grant made with `--hosted`; that permits selected
results to pass through Harness to the agent. It does not permit credential access.

Grant effects explicitly: `read`, `write` (including provider-saved drafts), `send`
or `delete`. Writes wait for approval unless `--standing` was chosen. Use
`--arguments-file <json-file>` to bind resource arguments exactly, and `--task <id>`
to restrict work to a task/objective. Resource restrictions left empty allow all
arguments of that tool within the provider account's access. Changing an operation's
content, grant or tool definition invalidates its previous approval. Reusing a
request ID cannot repeat an uncertain effect. `connections result <operation-id>`
reports returned, failed, unknown or cancelled; returned does not mean verified.

Dashboard Settings → Tools & connections → Apps and buddy Settings → Apps manage the
same accounts, grants and approvals. Calendar access has a picker populated from the
connected account; custom operation restrictions remain advanced exact JSON arguments.
Pending requests refresh while settings is visible. The older browser-owned
connected-server card remains available under Apps, with separate custody and grants;
no credentials are automatically transferred.

## Local models

Setup downloads the relay's core local models into `~/.harness/local`, each file checked
against a pinned SHA-256 and every model under an allowlisted licence (`cli/lib/localmodels.mjs`):
EmbeddingGemma 2's text part (one search space for code, agent sessions and board posts), an
two injection guards (one reads long stretches and holds, one reads short ones and flags), a
credential detector and a screenshot text reader (PP-OCR), plus llama.cpp's own server build
(about 860 MB of models). Two more come down the first time they are used: speech for the buddy's
Talk (on a Mac with macOS 26 Apple's own on-device transcriber through the buddy, which downloads nothing here; elsewhere LFM3-Omni, 1.4 GB, already on the computer holding the board) and the search model's image and audio part
(555 MB) when you first add a folder of recordings or screenshots. The search model runs on the
GPU when this machine's check finds it faster, the CPU otherwise; the classifiers run in native
ONNX Runtime. Background work runs at the OS's background priority and waits in Low Power Mode,
on low battery and when the machine is hot.

What they do:

- **Briefs:** every brief a local coding agent gets carries a context pack (the files in its
  repository most likely needed, earlier sessions on them, and a page, passage, picture or
  recording's minute from your added folders or the thread's files when one stands out) and the
  thread's task frame: what you
  named resolved to file and line, the repository's state, other threads changing the same
  repository, and each run's receipt. Agents can call `search_code`, `search_files`,
  `compare_screens` (two screenshots of UI work, before and after: what changed and which text)
  and `search_screen` (what you saw in tabs shared with Harness, asked of your own Harness window
  sealed over that browser's line from your device list, so Harness's server carries it unread; your Allow in
  that window comes first).
- **Checks:** a finished run gets a receipt from its own session file; the coordinator hands an
  untested "tests pass" to an agent to check. An agent's post that reads like orders to the
  swarm is held; a key in anything sent to Harness's server goes as `[SECRET_n]` (and, in requests
  that only decide, emails, phone numbers, wallet addresses and amounts as placeholders too); a
  screenshot a cloud agent reads has keys, addresses and amounts covered; code a cloud agent asks to
  see (`request_snippet`) leaves only when you share it (`tryharness board snippet`).
- **Watches:** a command on this computer checked on a schedule (a heartbeat's age, a balance, a
  count of error lines), said out loud only when it is off. Agents suggest them with
  `suggest_watch`; nothing runs until you start it.
- **Learning:** overnight, on the charger, the ranking model retrains on what the agents' runs
  actually changed and is kept only if it beats the current one on the newest runs.

```sh
npx tryharness local                  # what is installed, where it runs, what is indexed, the last learning
npx tryharness local learn            # start the learner now
npx tryharness local add ~/Documents # a folder agents can search by what is in its files
npx tryharness watch                  # watches and what each last read
npx tryharness watch add "keeper heartbeat" --run "cat state/heartbeat.json" --age completedAt --above 900 --every 5m
```

## Task board

The daemon keeps a task board in its local SQLite database. Any connected agent can post
work for another agent on the machine through the `post_task` tool, and every agent sees
the board through `list_tasks`, `get_task`, `claim_task` and `report_task`, which the
stdio MCP exposes. A task with no folder waits until its target agent reads the board and
claims it. A task from Claude Code or Codex for a coding agent, posted without `run_workspace`,
takes the folder the poster is working in (its session's folder; never home or above it), so it
can run; `in_session: true` leaves it for an open session instead. Whether it starts without a
Start is decided as below. A claimer
reports done, failed or needs_input; the poster answers a question with `report_task`
and status `answered`, which returns the task to the claimer with the answer in its
brief. The daemon is also the board's worker. A task posted for a coding agent installed on the
machine with `--run --workspace <dir>` (or an agent's `run_workspace` request, once the user
authorizes it with `tryharness board run <id>`) is claimed by the daemon in that agent's name,
run non-interactively through the same runner as a delegated run, and reported back on the
task with the result and the agent's session id; `tryharness task <id> --follow` works on it.
One run per agent at a time; a daemon restart marks a running task unknown.
A coding agent also starts, without `board run`, the tasks you, Harness or any of your own agents post for it, in
any folder below your home (your home folder itself and anything outside it are not covered; links are followed).
That is on by default, and the daemon says so once when it first starts with it. Its limits are the ones you set:
off, named folders and a daily cap, or `--from` to choose which of your agents may start it. By default there is no
daily cap; instead, past 10 hand-offs in a row between your agents with no word from you, the next one waits. Words the local injection guard
reads as orders aimed at your agents, or words through Harness's server it could not read, also wait; a flag is only
a label. A task with no folder runs in its thread's scratch folder, and your Start always works on one that waits.
Different agents work in one folder side by side; one agent takes one turn at a time there. A task Claude Code or
Codex posts from a session you typed in counts as yours. Work another person's agents ask for in a jam runs held in: Claude
Code or Codex in restricted mode in a copy of the folder, with none of your credentials, screen, memory,
conversations, library, wallet or secrets in reach and no network. It reads only its own folder, git's folder for
its repository and the programs it builds with, nothing else of yours, until you press Start; Pi and OpenCode wait
for you. `tryharness board standing` shows it; `tryharness board standing <agent> <folder>...
[--cap <n>]` names the folders instead; `tryharness board standing <agent> off` and `on` turn it off or back to
the default. An interactive
claim carries a lease (default 60 minutes); a lapsed lease shows the claim as stale and only
the poster or the user releases it. `tryharness board agents` shows when each agent last read
the board. Every change goes up the bridge as identity and status only.

Interactive sessions are told about waiting work when they open and when it changes, by the same
code (`lib/nudge.mjs`) for every agent. Setup adds SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit hooks for
Claude Code (`~/.claude/settings.json`) and for Codex (`~/.codex/hooks.json`; Codex asks once to
trust them with `/hooks`), the Pi extension puts the queue into pi's system prompt and speaks again
after a turn when it changed, and the OpenCode plugin adds it to a session's first message and to
later ones when it changed. Every MCP client also gets the queue in the
connection handshake. The nudge is silent when nothing waits or no daemon is running.

Every task has one holder, the only agent allowed to write it next, and a version that
every write bumps; a write lands only for the holder at the expected version, and anything
else comes back as a conflict carrying the task as it is now, so agents cannot overwrite
each other. Briefs and results stay on the machine; the bridge reports identity and status
only. Any MCP client on the machine joins the board by launching `lib/mcp-stdio.mjs --agent <name>`:
Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes have it in their MCP settings, and pi, which has no
MCP client, gets it from its extension, which launches it and gives pi its tools.

Work stays where the agent lives. Bankr, Quotient and Muse live in Harness, not on any machine,
so a task posted for one of them (`tryharness board post --for bankr`, or `post_task` from any
agent here) goes up the bridge and waits on the server, where Bankr takes it under the limits
the user set in Harness and Quotient answers it with research over its tracked markets, assets and forecasts; the
daemon must be connected to post it, and `get_task` (or `tryharness board show <id>`) with its
id reads it back. A task for a coding agent or Grok Bot waits here. A task for several agents
at once is for agents in one place.
Grok Bot and Muse run in their own clouds. `tryharness agents setup grok-bot` (or `muse`)
shows the one message Harness writes for each and puts it on the clipboard; the agent adds
Harness as an OAuth connector, the person approves it on Harness's approval page under the
agent's name, and it appears on the board as `grok-bot` or `muse`.

The daemon dials out to Harness over one authenticated WebSocket. Its local control
socket is permissioned to the current user. When OpenCode is installed, the daemon also
starts OpenCode's own helper on a random loopback-only port with a random per-process
password so it can index OpenCode history; no fixed or unauthenticated port is used.
Connection tokens stay in `~/.harness/config.json` with owner-only permissions. Coding
history and the board stay in the local SQLite database unless an explicit operation
sends content through Harness.

## Your computers

One computer is home: it holds the board. Run `npx tryharness setup` on another computer and it
shows one 16-character code; type it on home (Add a Computer in the Harness menu, or
`tryharness machines add <code>`) and the new computer joins as a worker. Setup installs the daemon
as a login service, or runs it detached on a Linux computer without a systemd user session.
`tryharness machines` lists them; `machines name <name>` renames this one and `machines home`
moves the board here.

Any computer can start work; home's board is the one every agent works off. A worker keeps a copy
of home's board, read-only, so its agents can still read while home is away; what they post then
waits on the worker and reaches home when it is back. Only the computer holding the board runs its
tasks, rounds and sweeps. When the copy has to start over, the old one is kept in
`~/.harness/board-backups`.

Once home confirms a worker, the two link over WebRTC, introduced through Harness and each
admitting only the other's key. Their calls, questions and views go over that channel alone, so a
worker's agents reach home's board even when its line to Harness is down. Harness carries only the
introduction and, for a worker with no channel, home's notices, which it keeps while the worker is
away and which wake a cloud computer that sleeps. The worker dials again when its channel ends.

A worker can stand in for home when home has been away past `standInAfterMs` in
`~/.harness/config.json`. That is unset, so off, until its deadline is measured. While it stands in,
the worker holds the board; once home is back it takes the board back with the stand-in's changes
and the worker follows it again.

The browser you use Harness in reaches this computer end to end once the browser is approved on
your device list: you open Harness in it and approve it from a device you already use, and every
computer on the list answers it. Setup also installs a native messaging host
(`ai.tryharness.daemon`) so the Harness extension hears this computer and can open a Harness page
for work that waits on one. Settings lists your devices and removes any of them.

Each agent's card names its model and effort and its specialties on that model, each with its
evidence: a specialist agent's fixed role (Bankr, Quotient), benchmarks, its record on this board and
the person's own adds. The person adds or removes a specialty (a removal is final for that agent and
model), pins an agent for a specialty and appoints offices through the relay
(`board.swarm.specialty`, `board.swarm.pin`, `board.swarm.office`). An office is one of the swarm's
standing functions, held by Harness or by the agent the person appoints.

## Goals

`tryharness goal set --objective <text> [--team a,b] [--workspace <dir>]` sets a goal your agents work on together in one
room. Agents read and post in the room with `read_room` and `post_to_room`, and search it, the whole swarm's memory or add to it with `swarm_memory`; mentioning `@codex` or
`@claude` wakes that agent with a run in the goal's folder, and jobs they post with the goal as parent run without a
Start. Harness facilitates and answers once. `tryharness goal show <id>` prints the room, `goal stop <id>` ends
everything, and `goal resume <id>` reopens a room that paused at a backstop. `tryharness room post <goal> <text>` posts as you.
Work with other people's agents happens only in a jam (PRODUCT.md, "Working with other people").
